claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a density greater than 11 g/cm³ because of its Hf and Zr content.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy fractures brittly at room temperature.
Limited active slip systems contribute to the baseline alloy's room-temperature brittleness.
Intermetallic precipitation may contribute to brittle failure in the baseline alloy.
Replacing 15-20 at.% of Hf and Zr with Nb or V will reduce the alloy's density.
Nb or V substitution combined with a specific Ti/Zr ratio will induce a metastable BCC solid solution.
Rapid solidification or severe plastic deformation will stabilize a metastable single-phase BCC structure in the modified alloy.
The stabilized BCC structure will have low stacking-fault energy.
The metastable BCC phase will transform to HCP or BCT under applied stress at room temperature.
Nanoscale coherent precipitates will impede dislocation motion and strengthen the modified alloy.
A balance between mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy will stabilize the proposed metastable phase.
Low stacking-fault energy will facilitate deformation twinning and martensite formation.
Stress-induced martensitic transformation will provide continuous work hardening through a TRIP effect.
Continuous work hardening will delay premature necking and fracture and thereby maintain ductility.
The modified alloy will have a room-temperature yield strength greater than 800 MPa.
The modified alloy will have room-temperature tensile ductility greater than 15%.
The modified alloy's bulk density will be at least 15% lower than that of the baseline alloy.
The proposed processing and substitution strategy can produce a density below 9.5 g/cm³.
Exceeding the substitution solubility limit will trigger brittle Laves phases or other complex intermetallics.
A sufficiently high cooling rate is required to retain the metastable phase.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies stabilization of a single-phase BCC structure, whereas the structural mediator requires nanoscale coherent precipitates. The hypothesis does not state that the precipitates form only later during deformation, leaving the proposed initial microstructure internally inconsistent.
